active_themes.label: Gulf Oil Slowly Returns
active_themes.summary: Brent rose 3.88% to $98.29 and WTI rose 2.72% to $90.52, giving back part of the recent drop while staying under $100. No deal is signed, and the Iran war is still being defended politically. The open question is whether Brent holds under $100 without physical proof that shipping through Hormuz is safer.

active_themes.label: Global Borrowing Costs Climb
active_themes.summary: The 10-year yield fell 0.06 points to 4.84% and the 30-year fell 0.03 points to 5.25% as some money fled stocks for government bonds. Yields remain high with inflation at 3.7%, so the relief is thin. The open question is whether the 10-year can fall toward 4.75% or oil pushes it back toward 5.00%.

active_themes.label: AI Spending Backlash
active_themes.summary: The Nasdaq's bounce was erased in one session: it fell 5.52% to 24,315 and entered correction territory. The most likely cause is a fear that a Democratic Congress and local data-center moratoriums will slow AI building, and retail investors sold more stock in one day than at any point since the Covid sell-off. The open question is whether the Nasdaq can climb back above 25,000 or breaks below 24,000, which would mean investors are repricing AI rather than panicking.

active_themes.label: Democratic Sweep Reaction
active_themes.summary: The first read of the Democratic sweep was relief, as a brake on tariffs, the war and pressure on the Fed. Today's session turned that around: the same result is now being priced as a regulatory threat to the AI industry that leads the market. The open question is whether the political check is a net positive for markets or whether tech's losses outweigh the relief elsewhere.

active_themes.label: Fed Eyes Another Hike
active_themes.summary: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin both favor gradual rate hikes because inflation stays high, and the Bank of England raised its rate to 4% from 3.75% with another rise signaled. A 4% stock drop did not change that tone, so there is no sign of a central-bank rescue. The open question is whether oil stays low enough to take a December Fed hike off the table.

active_themes.label: Iran War Resumption Risk
active_themes.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and oil still fell sharply. Markets are treating the diplomatic and political track as stronger than the incidents. The open question is whether these fires become a pattern of sustained attacks on shipping, which would erase today's oil drop.

Bond buyers finally believe cheaper oil will last, which would be the first real sign of relief on borrowing costs.
The longest borrowing costs would be pushing meaningfully higher, deepening the strain on mortgages, stocks and company borrowing.
Bond buyers are ignoring cheaper oil and today's yield relief has failed.
Today's sell-off was mostly forced selling, and the AI trade is stabilizing.
Fear has moved from elevated to panic, which tends to mean more forced selling before a bottom.
Renewed inflation pressure makes a Fed hike more likely and removes the one cushion stocks could still lean on.
